title: New pornography offences in the UK
subtitle: What Part 5, Chapter 4 of the Crime and Policing Act 2026 actually criminalises, where it applies, and where the participant defences leave a gap.
summary: From 6 November 2026, England and Wales has three new offences of possessing or publishing certain pornographic images: strangulation or suffocation; penetrative sex between people a reasonable person would think are, or are pretending to be, related; and sexual activity where a reasonable person would think at least one person is, or is pretending to be, under 16. A Scottish strangulation offence remains prospective and, once in force, will be stricter. The new offences largely target third-party possession and publication beyond the participants. They sit inside a wider body of criminal and regulatory law: a defence or exception to one offence is not a declaration that the conduct is lawful. A labelled “cheeky table” at the end tests two edge cases against the statutory scope of the imagery offences. This is legal research, not legal advice, and it is not a guide to producing any image.
scope: United Kingdom, with the territorial differences set out below. Sections 104, 106 and 107 of the Crime and Policing Act 2026 are in force in England and Wales from 6 November 2026. Section 104 also extends to Northern Ireland but has not been commenced there. Section 105, for Scotland, is not in force. If an image depicts a person who is actually under 18, the Protection of Children Act 1978, section 160 of the Criminal Justice Act 1988 and related offences apply in addition to anything on this page.
status_note: The statutes and commencement instruments cited were read from legislation.gov.uk on 23 November 2026. The CPS Obscene Publications guidance was read the same day. This is legal research and commentary, not legal advice.

highlights.label: In force
highlights.detail: Sections 104, 106 and 107 are in force in England and Wales. The Scottish strangulation offence remains prospective.

highlights.label: The recording gap
highlights.detail: For some role-play cases the new offences do not ban a participant’s private recording. They ban possession by others, and publication beyond the participants. Other offences may still apply.

highlights.label: Scotland
highlights.detail: Once section 105 is in force, a recording of real strangulation has no participant defence in Scotland, even if the act was consensual and caused no injury.

highlights.label: Section 98
highlights.detail: The enacted offence of sharing a semen-defaced image has not been commenced. Only a related Online Safety Act amendment was brought in on 29 June 2026.

sections.title: Sources and legislation
sections.intro: The claims on this page are taken from the official text, and from Crown Prosecution Service guidance and contemporaneous reporting where that is stated. Each link goes to the source cited.

paragraphs.text: Part 5, Chapter 4 of the Crime and Policing Act 2026 is the pornography chapter. The offence-creating sections are section 104, section 105, section 106 and section 107. Extent is set out in section 254. The Commencement No. 4 Regulations brought sections 104(1) to (3), so far as they extend to England and Wales, and sections 106 and 107, into force on 6 November 2026.

links.text: Part 5, Chapter 4 of the Crime and Policing Act 2026

paragraphs.text: Section 98 and Schedule 13 deal with semen-defaced images and related intimate-image amendments. Section 99 inserts an offence of making or supplying a purported intimate image generator. Section 113, in force from 29 September 2026, restates the exposure offence in section 66 of the Sexual Offences Act 2003.

The new offences use the definition of a “pornographic” image in section 63 of the Criminal Justice and Immigration Act 2008, and the definition of “non-consensual harm” in section 66(3) of that Act. Section 63 remains the extreme-pornography possession offence. Section 75A of the Serious Crime Act 2015 is the offline offence of strangulation or suffocation in England and Wales.

links.text: section 63 of the Criminal Justice and Immigration Act 2008
Section 75A of the Serious Crime Act 2015

paragraphs.text: Sections 64 and 65 of the Sexual Offences Act 2003 criminalise penetrative sex between listed adult blood and adoptive relatives. Section 66 of that Act is the exposure offence. Section 66A is the offence of sending a photograph or film of genitals. Section 66B covers sharing, or threatening to share, an intimate photograph or film. Section 66E, inserted by section 138 of the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 and in force from 6 February 2026, is the offence of creating a purported intimate image of an adult; section 66F, in force from the same date, covers requesting such a creation. Sections 67 and 67A are the voyeurism offences. Section 62 of the Coroners and Justice Act 2009 is the offence of possessing a prohibited non-photographic image of a child; section 65 of that Act defines “image” and “child”. The Obscene Publications Act 1959, section 2, criminalises publication of an obscene article; having an obscene article for publication for gain is covered by the 1964 Act.

paragraphs.text: Other statutes that can apply to the same facts include section 127 of the Communications Act 2003, section 1 of the Malicious Communications Act 1988, the Protection of Children Act 1978, section 160 of the Criminal Justice Act 1988, the Protection from Harassment Act 1997, sections 44 to 46 of the Serious Crime Act 2007, the false and threatening communications offences in sections 179 and 181 of the Online Safety Act 2023, and the Indecent Displays (Control) Act 1981. Section 189 of the 2023 Act, in force from 31 January 2024, repealed only some limbs of the 2003 and 1988 communications offences in England, Wales and Northern Ireland.

paragraphs.text: The Crown Prosecution Service Obscene Publications guidance, as read on 23 November 2026, lists the new 6 November 2026 offences. It also lists, as possible offences for prosecutors to consider, a number of the older possession, communications, harassment, display and inchoate offences set out later on this page. The published page does not itself state a November 2026 revision date. On the 1959 Act, the guidance says that a prosecution is not likely where the conduct is consensual, no serious harm is caused, the conduct is not inextricably linked with other criminality, and the likely audience is not under 18 or otherwise vulnerable.

paragraphs.text: On 6 January 2012 a jury at Southwark Crown Court acquitted Michael Peacock of six charges under the Obscene Publications Act arising from the sale of DVDs to an undercover officer. BBC News and The Guardian reported the unanimous not guilty verdicts. The Guardian reported that the material included so-called “water-sports” and other acts that are legal between consenting adults.

sections.title: The offences
sections.intro: Four sections add possession and publication offences for certain pornographic images. They sit alongside the older extreme-pornography offence, not in place of it. Shared machinery is set out first; each section then has its own elements, participant defence, extent, commencement and penalties.

paragraphs.text: Each provision creates a possession offence and a publication offence. An image is pornographic if it must reasonably be assumed to have been produced solely or principally for the purpose of sexual arousal, the definition in section 63 of the 2008 Act. Publishing includes giving or making the image available to another person by any means. The offences do not apply to excluded images within the meaning of section 64 of the 2008 Act or, in Scotland once section 105 is in force, section 51B of the Civic Government (Scotland) Act 1982. In England and Wales, proceedings may not be instituted except by or with the consent of the Director of Public Prosecutions.

For sections 104, 106 and 107, and for the Scottish offence once in force, a reasonable person looking at the image must think that the persons were real. Section 106 and section 107 also take into account any sound or information associated with the image. The same “real person” test appears in section 63 of the 2008 Act.

There are defences of legitimate reason; of not having seen the image and having no cause to suspect its character; and, for possession, of having been sent it unsolicited and not keeping it for an unreasonable time. A further defence is available to a person who directly participated in the act, on conditions that differ by section and are set out below. For publication, that participant defence also requires that the image was published only to the other participant or participants. Where the defence refers to “non-consensual harm”, the phrase has the meaning in section 66(3) of the 2008 Act, set out under existing law below.

entries.title: Section 104: strangulation or suffocation (England and Wales, and Northern Ireland)

paragraphs.text: Section 104 inserts sections 67A to 67D into the 2008 Act. It is an offence to possess or publish a pornographic image that portrays, in an explicit and realistic way, a person strangling or suffocating another person.
The participant defence is available if the person directly participated in the act portrayed and the act did not involve the infliction of any non-consensual harm on any person.

Subsections (1) to (3) extend to England and Wales and Northern Ireland. They have been in force in England and Wales since 6 November 2026, and only so far as they extend to England and Wales. They have not been commenced in Northern Ireland. The Online Safety Act amendment in subsection (5) extends to the whole United Kingdom and came into force on the same date.

On conviction on indictment, possession carries a maximum of two years, and publication a maximum of five years. Once the offence is in force in Northern Ireland, the consent of the Director of Public Prosecutions for Northern Ireland would be required.

Section 105 would insert sections 51D to 51G into the Civic Government (Scotland) Act 1982. It is an offence to possess or publish a pornographic image that depicts, in an explicit and realistic way, a person strangling or suffocating another person. The section extends to Scotland only. It is not in force.

sources.locator: s.105(1), inserting s.51D; commencement note I1

paragraphs.text: The participant defence is available only if the person directly participated and “the act did not actually involve strangulation or suffocation of any person”. A recording of real strangulation would have no participant defence in Scotland, even if the act was consensual and caused no injury. That is stricter than the England and Wales defence under section 67B.
Once the section is in force, the indictment maxima would be two years for possession and five years for publication.

Section 106 inserts sections 67E to 67G. The image must be pornographic and must portray, in an explicit and realistic way, sexual penetration of the vagina or anus with a body part or anything else, or of the mouth by a penis. A reasonable person must think the people were real, and — taking into account any associated sound or information — that they were related, or pretending to be related, in a listed way. For blood and adoptive relationships (parent, grandparent, child, grandchild, brother, sister, half-brother, half-sister, uncle, aunt, nephew or niece) the offence is not limited by age. For step and foster relationships, at least one person must be, or be pretending to be, under 18. A fanciful pretence of relationship is excluded.
The participant defence requires direct participation, no non-consensual harm, and that the person was not, and had not been, related to the other person in a listed way.

The offence itself extends to England and Wales only, and came into force on 6 November 2026. Subsections (2) and (3), certain ancillary provisions, extend to England and Wales and Northern Ireland. The Online Safety Act amendment in subsection (7) extends to the whole United Kingdom.
On conviction on indictment, possession carries a maximum of two years, and publication a maximum of five years.

entries.title: Section 107: sexual activity with a person under 16, or pretended to be under 16

paragraphs.text: Section 107 inserts sections 67H to 67J. The statutory heading is “Pornographic images of sexual activity with child under 16”. Possession or publication is an offence where a reasonable person, looking at a pornographic image and taking into account any associated sound or information, would think that it portrays, in an explicit and realistic way, sexual activity between two people who are real, and that at least one of them is, or is pretending to be, under 16. Penetration is not required. A person is not to be taken as pretending to be under 16 if it is fanciful that they actually are under 16 in the way pretended.

The participant defence requires direct participation, no non-consensual harm, and that neither person was actually under 16. If anyone depicted is actually under 18, the Protection of Children Act 1978, section 160 of the Criminal Justice Act 1988 and related offences already apply. Section 107 does not replace them. This page discusses the statutory treatment of adult role-play imagery. It is not a guide to producing any image, and it is not about sexual images of actual children.

The offence itself extends to England and Wales only, and came into force on 6 November 2026. Subsections (2) and (3), certain ancillary provisions, extend to England and Wales and Northern Ireland. The Online Safety Act amendment in subsection (5) extends to the whole United Kingdom. On conviction on indictment, possession carries a maximum of three years, and publication a maximum of five years.

sections.title: Not prohibited here ≠ lawful everywhere
sections.intro: A defence or exception to one offence is not a declaration that the conduct is lawful. The 2026 imagery offences sit inside a much larger body of law. The rows that follow are potential legal issues, not automatic offences whenever sexual material is involved.

entries.title: A gap in one offence is not a declaration of legality

paragraphs.text: A defence or exception to one criminal offence is not a general declaration that the conduct is lawful. The new imagery offences sit alongside older possession, assault, sexual, communications and publication offences. The Home Office factsheet on the 2026 Act treats those new offences as additions to an existing regime, including the indecent-images-of-children offences, and states that they will be listed as priority offences under the Online Safety Act 2023.

links.text: Home Office factsheet on the 2026 Act

paragraphs.text: Prosecution guidance is not a statutory defence. The current CPS test for a prosecution under the 1959 Act, set out under sources above, indicates that a prosecution is not likely in particular consensual circumstances. That is a statement about charging practice. It does not mean that Parliament has made the material categorically lawful.

table.caption: A way of checking whether conduct that falls outside one of the 2026 imagery offences is still criminal under another provision. The stages can overlap, and more than one offence can apply to the same facts.
rows: 1. Underlying act
Consent, age, coercion, violence, injury — including whether the act itself is a sexual or assault offence, quite apart from any image.
2. Image creation
Recording, voyeurism, AI generation, and privacy: was the image made, requested, or generated, and with whose consent?
3. Possession
Who has the image, and does a possession offence apply — including extreme pornography, prohibited images of children, and the 2026 possession offences?
4. Distribution or communication
Publication, sending, sharing, display, or other communication — including obscenity, communications offences, and intimate-image offences.

paragraphs.text: For each potentially applicable offence, the useful questions are the statutory elements, the mental element, the available defences or exceptions, territorial extent, commencement, relevant case law, and prosecution guidance.

Section 63 of the 2008 Act remains the offence of possessing an extreme pornographic image. An “extreme image” must be grossly offensive, disgusting or otherwise of an obscene character, and must fall within a closed list. Subsection (7) covers acts that threaten a person’s life; acts that result, or are likely to result, in serious injury to a person’s anus, breasts or genitals; sexual interference with a human corpse; and intercourse or oral sex with an animal. Subsection (7A) covers two forms of non-consensual penetration. In each case a reasonable person looking at the image must think the people, or the person or animal, were real. Bodily fluids are not a listed category.

The participant defences in sections 67B, 67F and 67I use the definition in section 66(3) of the 2008 Act. Harm inflicted on a person is “non-consensual” harm if (a) the harm is of such a nature that the person cannot, in law, consent to it being inflicted on himself or herself; or (b) where the person can, in law, consent to it being so inflicted, the person does not in fact consent to it being so inflicted.

Section 75A of the Serious Crime Act 2015 makes it an offence in England and Wales intentionally to strangle another person, or to do any other act that affects the person’s ability to breathe and constitutes battery. Consent is a defence, but that defence does not apply if the person suffers “serious harm” and the defendant intended that harm or was reckless as to it. “Serious harm” is defined as grievous bodily harm, wounding, or actual bodily harm. The consent defence is evidential: sufficient evidence must be adduced to raise the issue, and the prosecution must then disprove it beyond reasonable doubt.

That is the offline statutory baseline that the England and Wales pornography participant defence appears designed to track. The two tests are not worded identically. Whether a given injury that would defeat the section 75A consent defence also amounts to “non-consensual harm” under section 66(3) would be a question for a court.

entries.title: Sex with an adult relative: sections 64 and 65

paragraphs.text: Sections 64 and 65 of the Sexual Offences Act 2003 make it an offence for a person aged 16 or over to penetrate, or to consent to being penetrated by, a listed adult blood or adoptive relative, knowing or being reasonably expected to know of the relationship. The listed relationships are the same blood and adoptive relationships used in section 106. Step and foster relationships are not included. The offline offences require sexual penetration; they do not apply merely because two adults are step or foster relatives, both 18 or over.

Section 66 of the Sexual Offences Act 2003 is titled “Exposure”, not “indecent exposure”. From 29 September 2026, a person who intentionally exposes their genitals commits the offence if they intend that someone will see the genitals and be caused alarm, distress or humiliation, or if they expose them for sexual gratification with the intention that someone will see them and being reckless as to whether someone who sees them will be caused alarm, distress or humiliation. Common-law outraging public decency is a separate offence.

Section 66B makes it an offence to share, or threaten to share, a photograph or film that shows, or appears to show, another person in an intimate state, without consent. Section 66E, in force from 6 February 2026, makes it an offence to create a purported intimate image of an adult without consent and without a reasonable belief in consent. Section 66F, in force from the same date, makes it an offence to request the creation of such an image, or to request that it include or exclude something in particular, without consent and without a reasonable belief in consent. The request offence is committed whether or not the image is ever created, and there is a reasonable-excuse defence. Section 99 of the 2026 Act, in force from 29 June 2026, is a different offence: it inserts section 66I, which criminalises making or supplying a thing for use as a generator of purported intimate images.

Section 66A, in force from 31 January 2024, is the cyberflashing offence: intentionally sending or giving a photograph or film of any person’s genitals, including a computer-generated image that appears to be such a photograph or film, with the intention that the recipient will see the genitals and be caused alarm, distress or humiliation, or for sexual gratification while reckless as to those effects. Sections 67 and 67A criminalise voyeurism, including recording a person doing a private act without consent for sexual gratification, and additional offences of recording beneath clothing or while a person is breastfeeding.

Schedule 13, paragraph 2 of the 2026 Act would insert a new section 66AA, “Sharing semen-defaced image”. A person would commit an offence by intentionally sharing a semen-defaced image of another person, without that person’s consent, and without a reasonable belief in consent. A “semen-defaced image” is a photograph or film which shows, or appears to show, that person and which has, or appears to have, semen on it or in its immediate vicinity, or a photograph or film of such an image. There is a reasonable-excuse defence, and an exception where the image had already been publicly shared with consent. It would be a summary-only offence. The offence is the sharing, not a private act between consenting participants. As at 23 November 2026 the provision remains prospective. On 29 June 2026, section 98 was commenced only so far as it relates to Schedule 13, paragraph 24, an Online Safety Act amendment.

table.caption: Potential legal issues, not automatic offences whenever sexual material is involved. Rows for statutes already discussed above are kept short. “Distribution” here includes publication, sending, sharing and public display. Links follow the table.
rows: Obscene Publications Act 1959, s.2
Distribution

Publishing an obscene article, meaning its effect is such as to tend to deprave and corrupt persons likely to read, see or hear it. Private possession is not an offence. Having an article for publication for gain is covered by the 1964 Act, which also amends s.2.
Publication is a deliberate act. Obscenity is the statutory “deprave and corrupt” test, not the ordinary meaning of “obscene”.

A defence if the person has not examined the article and had no reasonable cause to suspect it was obscene (s.2(5)). Public-good defence in s.4 (science, literature, art or learning, or other objects of general concern). CPS charging guidance is not a defence.
England and Wales. In force. The Act does not extend to Scotland or Northern Ireland.
Communications Act 2003, s.127(1)
Distribution / communication

Sending, by a public electronic communications network, a message or other matter that is grossly offensive or of an indecent, obscene or menacing character. The offence is limited to that network. Section 127(2)(c) still covers persistently making use of such a network to cause annoyance, inconvenience or needless anxiety.
Intention that the message be of the prohibited character, or awareness that it may be so (DPP v Collins).
No general statutory defence. The public-network limit is an element of the offence.

United Kingdom for s.127(1) and s.127(2)(c). In force. From 31 January 2024, s.127(2)(a) and (b) (false messages) are repealed in England, Wales and Northern Ireland only; those limbs remain in force in Scotland.
Malicious Communications Act 1988, s.1
Distribution / communication

Sending a letter, electronic communication or article that conveys an indecent or grossly offensive message, or that is itself indecent or grossly offensive, if a purpose of sending it is to cause distress or anxiety to the recipient or to someone the sender intends it to reach. It is not limited to a public electronic communications network.
Purpose, or one of the purposes, of causing distress or anxiety.
No general statutory defence in the remaining provision.

England and Wales. In force. Does not extend to Scotland. From 31 January 2024 the limbs covering a threat, and information known or believed to be false, and the associated subsection (2), are repealed. Northern Ireland has a separate Order, similarly amended.
Criminal Justice and Immigration Act 2008, s.63
Possession
Possession of an extreme pornographic image, under the closed list set out above. Bodily fluids are not a listed category.
Possession. The image must be pornographic and of an obscene character, and a reasonable person looking at it must think the people, or the person or animal, were real.
Defences in sections 64 to 66, including the participant defence and the non-consensual-harm limit set out above.
England, Wales and Northern Ireland. In force.
Protection of Children Act 1978, s.1
Creation; possession with a view to distribution; distribution

Taking, making, distributing, showing, possessing with a view to distribution, or advertising indecent photographs or pseudo-photographs of a child (a person under 18). “Making” includes downloading an image.
The acts are intentional; whether an image is indecent is a question of fact.
Statutory defences include a legitimate reason, lack of knowledge or cause to suspect indecency in some cases, and limited marriage and civil-partnership exceptions.
England and Wales. In force. If an image depicts a person who is actually under 18, these offences apply in addition to the 2026 imagery offences.
Criminal Justice Act 1988, s.160
Possession
Simple possession of an indecent photograph or pseudo-photograph of a child.
Possession, with knowledge-related defences.
Legitimate reason; no knowledge or suspicion; unsolicited receipt where the image is not kept; limited marriage and civil-partnership exceptions.
England and Wales. In force.
Coroners and Justice Act 2009, s.62
Possession
Possession of a prohibited non-photographic image of a child, as set out above, including an imaginary child. There is no “reasonable person would think the person was real” requirement.
Possession. The image must be pornographic, of a listed kind, and grossly offensive, disgusting or otherwise of an obscene character.
Section 64, including legitimate reason, no knowledge, and an exclusion for certain classified films.
England, Wales and Northern Ireland. In force.
Sexual Offences Act 2003, s.66B
Distribution
Sharing, or threatening to share, a photograph or film that shows or appears to show another person in an intimate state, without consent, as set out above.
Intention to share or to threaten. Some forms of the offence require an intention to cause alarm, distress or humiliation, or that the act is done for sexual gratification.
Absence of consent, and absence of a reasonable belief in consent, are elements. Further exceptions are set out in the surrounding sections.
England and Wales. In force from 31 January 2024.
Sexual Offences Act 2003, ss.66E–66F
Creation

Section 66E: creating a purported intimate image of an adult without consent, as set out above. Section 66F: intentionally requesting the creation of such an image, or requesting that it include or exclude something in particular. The request offence is committed whether or not the image is created, and wherever in the world the person requested is located.
Intention to create or to request; no consent and no reasonable belief in consent.
Section 66F has a reasonable-excuse defence. Consent and reasonable belief in consent are elements of both offences.
England and Wales. In force from 6 February 2026.
Sexual Offences Act 2003, ss.67–67A
Creation / observation

Section 67: voyeurism, including observing or recording a person doing a private act, or operating or installing equipment for that purpose. Section 67A: additional offences of operating equipment or recording an image beneath a person’s clothing, and of observing or recording a person who is breastfeeding.

Section 67 requires a purpose of obtaining sexual gratification and knowledge that the person does not consent. Section 67A requires a purpose of sexual gratification, or of humiliating, alarming or distressing the person, and no consent and no reasonable belief in consent.
The consent elements are built into the offences as set out in the previous column.
England and Wales. Section 67 is in force. Section 67A has been in force since 12 April 2019; the breastfeeding limbs since 28 June 2022.
Sexual Offences Act 2003, s.66A
Distribution / communication

Cyberflashing: intentionally sending or giving a photograph or film of any person’s genitals, including a computer-generated image that appears to be such a photograph or film, or showing it or placing it for a particular person to find. This is a Sexual Offences Act offence, inserted by section 187 of the Online Safety Act 2023; it is not a section of the 2023 Act.
Intention that the recipient will see the genitals and be caused alarm, distress or humiliation; or sending for sexual gratification, reckless as to those effects.
No general statutory defence in section 66A.
England and Wales. In force from 31 January 2024.
Protection from Harassment Act 1997, ss.2 and 4
Distribution / communication (and other courses of conduct)

Section 2: pursuing a course of conduct (at least two occasions) that amounts to harassment of another, which includes alarming a person or causing them distress. Section 4: a course of conduct that causes another to fear, on at least two occasions, that violence will be used against them.
The person knows, or ought to know (a reasonable-person test), that the conduct amounts to harassment, or will cause that fear of violence.

Preventing or detecting crime; acting under a legal requirement; and, for section 2, that the pursuit was reasonable, or for section 4, that it was reasonable for the protection of the person or another or of property.
England and Wales. In force.
Common-law outraging public decency
Underlying act / public display

A lewd, obscene or disgusting act, of such a character as to outrage public decency, done in a place where there is a real possibility that at least two members of the public might witness it. The two people need not actually have seen it, or have been outraged.
A deliberate act. The outraging character is assessed objectively.
No general statutory defence. A purely private act is not this offence.
Common law of England and Wales. In force.
Serious Crime Act 2007, ss.44–46
Inchoate liability at any stage

Doing an act capable of encouraging or assisting an offence: with intent to encourage or assist it (s.44); believing that the offence will be committed and that the act will encourage or assist it (s.45); or believing that one or more of a number of offences will be committed (s.46). Intention is not inferred merely because encouragement or assistance was a foreseeable consequence (s.44(2)).
As in the three sections: intent (s.44), or the stated beliefs (ss.45–46).
A defence of acting reasonably, in circumstances known or reasonably believed (s.50).
England, Wales and Northern Ireland. In force from 1 October 2008.
Online Safety Act 2023, ss.179 and 181
Distribution / communication

Section 179: sending a message conveying information the sender knows to be false, intending that it cause non-trivial psychological or physical harm to a likely audience, with no reasonable excuse. Section 181: sending a message conveying a threat of death or serious harm — grievous bodily harm, rape, assault by penetration, or serious financial loss.

Section 179 requires knowledge of falsity and an intention to cause that harm. Section 181 requires intention, or recklessness, as to whether someone encountering the message would fear that the threat would be carried out.
Section 179 includes a “no reasonable excuse” element. These offences replaced the repealed false and threat limbs of the 1988 and 2003 Acts in England, Wales and Northern Ireland.
England, Wales and Northern Ireland. In force from 31 January 2024. They do not extend to Scotland.
Indecent Displays (Control) Act 1981, s.1
Distribution (public display)

Publicly displaying indecent matter, or causing or permitting such a display. Matter displayed in, or so as to be visible from, a public place is deemed publicly displayed. The human body itself is not “matter”.
Making, causing or permitting the display. “Indecent” is not defined in the Act.

Exceptions for certain paid-admission displays and shop areas behind an adequate warning notice, if people under 18 are not admitted; and specified exceptions for television, museums and galleries, Crown or local-authority buildings, plays, and licensed film exhibitions.
England, Wales and Scotland. In force from 27 October 1981. It does not extend to Northern Ireland.

paragraphs.text: Obscene publication is not the same as grossly offensive communication. The 1959 Act asks whether the article tends to deprave and corrupt those likely to read, see or hear it. Section 127 of the 2003 Act is about the character of a communication and the circumstances of sending it over a public electronic communications network. Something can be offensive without being criminally grossly offensive. In DPP v Collins the House of Lords held that a message is grossly offensive if it would be so regarded by reasonable persons in society, judged by the standards of an open and just multi-racial society, and that the sender must have intended it to be so or have been aware that it might be. The CPS notes that where another offence uses the word “obscene” but does not define it, the ordinary meaning applies, not the “deprave and corrupt” test.

Consensual conduct is not necessarily lawful conduct. Non-fatal strangulation, actual bodily harm, grievous bodily harm, coercion and sexual offences can raise separate criminal liability even where everyone involved says they agreed. Consent does not automatically resolve every offence: the section 75A baseline, and the non-consensual-harm limit in the participant defences, are examples already set out above. Equally, a fictional depiction does not establish that the underlying conduct actually occurred.

Private possession, creation and publication are legally distinct. An image may be lawful for one participant to possess under a specific statutory defence, while publication of the same image beyond the participants is prohibited. That is the point of the participant-defence analysis on this page. Conversely, the communications offences require sending a message or article; they do not generally criminalise merely keeping material privately. Private possession is also outside the 1959 Act. The 2012 Peacock acquittal is consistent with the current CPS approach to that Act. Whether any given publication would be charged remains a fact-specific decision.

These are not additional criminal offences in the same sense as the rows above, but they affect the analysis. Article 10 of the European Convention on Human Rights protects freedom of expression; Article 8 protects private and family life. Both are given effect in domestic law by the Human Rights Act 1998. Public authorities, including prosecutors, must act compatibly with those rights. The CPS Obscene Publications guidance treats Article 10 as engaged by an alleged obscene publication, and says a prosecution may be compatible where it is prescribed by law and necessary and proportionate for the prevention of disorder or crime, or for the protection of health or morals.

Intimate images of identifiable people are personal data. Data concerning a person’s sexual life is a special category of personal data under Article 9 of the UK GDPR, as supplemented by the Data Protection Act 2018. That is a regulatory regime for processing, not a substitute for the criminal offences.

The Online Safety Act 2023 also imposes duties on platforms, distinct from the user-facing communications offences. Section 81, in Part 5, requires providers of regulated provider pornographic content to use highly effective age verification or age estimation so that children are not normally able to encounter that content. That duty has been in force since 17 January 2025. The Home Office factsheet states that the 2026 imagery offences will be listed as priority offences under the same Act, which would engage the illegal-content duties on in-scope services.

When Parliament creates a narrowly defined prohibition, how can someone tell whether conduct outside that prohibition is nevertheless criminal under another provision? The short answer is that they cannot treat the gap as a safe harbour. They have to ask, for each other offence that might apply, what the statutory elements are, what mental element must be proved, what defences or exceptions exist, where the offence extends, whether it is in force, what the case law does with the words, and what the prosecution guidance says — remembering that guidance is not itself a defence.

sections.title: Do versus record
sections.intro: The new offences largely do not criminalise a participant’s private recording of an act that was lawful to perform, subject to the non-consensual-harm limit in England and Wales and to the “no actual strangulation” limit in Scotland once section 105 is in force. They criminalise possession by third parties and publication beyond the participants. Whether another offence also applies is a separate question, taken up in the overlapping-offences analysis above.

paragraphs.text: For actual blood or adoptive relatives in a listed relationship, there is no “lawful to do, lawful to record, criminal to share” gap: the offline penetrative act is already an offence, and the participant defence to the imagery offence is unavailable. For the role-play cases, that gap is the point of the participant defence. Other offences — including those protecting children, section 63, the Obscene Publications Act, and public-place offences — may still apply on particular facts.

Possession is, in principle, a continuing act. An image still held after 6 November 2026 can be possessed on or after that date even if it was first acquired earlier. That is the ordinary reading of a possession offence. We found no transitional exemption in the Commencement No. 4 Regulations, and no official guidance on cloud backups, caches or shared accounts.

sections.title: Cheeky table
sections.intro: Two edge cases, tested against the statutes set out above. The conclusions are about statutory scope, not a prediction of any charging decision or verdict, and not a statement that a gap in one offence is a safe harbour from every other offence.

paragraphs.text: We do not suggest, we do not advocate, we do not support, we do not find enjoyable in any way, shape or form. The point of the “cheeky table” is to analyse and fine-tune the existing gaps that were left there on purpose. Or maybe by accident? Anyway, that’s the law. Talking about the law should not be an offence.

entries.title: Consenting adults, private premises, no penetration

paragraphs.text: On the face of the statutes, neither Chapter 4 nor section 63 criminalises consenting adults, in private, engaging in mutual masturbation or in activity involving bodily fluids, including semen or urine, where no listed act is portrayed. Sections 104 and 107 are not engaged if there is no strangulation or suffocation, and no portrayal of a person who is, or is pretending to be, under 16. Section 106 is not engaged, even if the people were framed as biological siblings, because that offence requires sexual penetration. Fluids are not a listed category under section 63.

Two traps sit elsewhere on the statute book. First, if section 66AA is commenced, sharing a semen-defaced image of another person without consent would be a summary offence, as set out above. A private recording of consenting participants is not that offence. Second, venue matters. Exposure under section 66 requires the mental elements already stated; it is not made out automatically merely because the setting is a public swimming pool. Outraging public decency is a separate common-law offence.
Private possession is outside the 1959 Act. A publication of this kind of material would be assessed under the current CPS test set out above.

entries.title: An AI-generated fictional adult with additional breasts

paragraphs.text: An AI-generated erotic image of a fictional adult with four breasts sits outside Chapter 4 and section 63 if the “real person” test is not met, and in any event four breasts, without more, are not a listed act under section 63, section 67A, section 67E or section 67H. Whether a particular image would fail the “real person” test is a question of fact, not a rule of law. It can be argued that a torso with four breasts would not be taken by a reasonable person as a real human being. A prosecutor might invite a different conclusion by reference to rare congenital conditions.

Three other offences can still apply. Section 62 of the Coroners and Justice Act 2009 — possession of a prohibited image of a child — has no “reasonable person would think the person was real” requirement. A “child” is a person under 18, including an imaginary child. Where an image shows a person, it is to be treated as an image of a child if the impression conveyed is that the person shown is a child, or if that is the predominant impression even though some of the physical characteristics shown are not those of a child. Fantasy anatomy does not, by itself, take an image outside section 62 if the character is depicted as under 18. The image must still be pornographic, fall within the listed forms of content, and be grossly offensive, disgusting or otherwise of an obscene character.

Creating or sharing a purported intimate image of a real, identifiable person without consent is already a crime, whether or not the image also alters the person’s anatomy: that is sections 66E and 66B, not section 99. And if a generated image passed the “appears real” test and also portrayed a listed extreme act — for example an act involving a human corpse, an animal, or non-consensual penetration — section 63 would be capable of applying to that act.

paragraphs.text: The scorecard is about statutory scope. It is not legal advice, and it is not a statement that any image or act is lawful in every respect. A gap in one offence is not a safe harbour from the others.
